stem:
A 68-year-old man has bone pain and an enlarging, deforming skull, and studies show markedly elevated osteoclast activity.

His weak, fracture-prone bones result from a remodeling imbalance in which his osteoclasts do which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Deposit excess collagen matrix on the periosteum
options.misconception: A formative action is being assigned to osteoclasts.
options.explanation: Osteoclasts resorb bone; deposition of collagen matrix is the work of osteoblasts at the periosteum and endosteum.

options.label: B
options.text: Trap osteoblasts inside the calcified matrix
options.misconception: The osteocyte transition is being attributed to osteoclasts.
options.explanation: Osteoblasts trap THEMSELVES as the matrix they secrete calcifies, becoming osteocytes; osteoclasts play no part in that transition.

options.label: C
options.text: Convert compact bone into hyaline cartilage
options.misconception: Resorption is being cast as a tissue conversion.
options.explanation: Osteoclasts break down bone matrix; they do not convert bone into any other tissue.

options.label: D
options.text: Stimulate osteoblasts to form extra lamellae
options.misconception: The compensatory response is being cast as the primary defect.
options.explanation: The primary defect is excessive osteoclast resorption; osteoblast compensation follows but produces weak, brittle bone, not healthy extra lamellae.

options.label: E
options.text: Resorb more bone than the osteoblasts lay down
options.misconception: None; overactive resorption outpaces formation, leaving weak bone.
options.explanation: This is Paget's disease: a remodeling disorder beginning with overactive osteoclasts, so more bone is resorbed than laid down; the compensating osteoblasts lay down weak, brittle bone prone to fracture.

context: Learning objective: remodeling balance. Osteoclasts resorb unneeded, damaged, or old bone while osteoblasts lay down new bone. Paget's disease begins with overactive osteoclasts — resorption outpaces formation, and compensatory osteoblast activity lays down weak, brittle bone (pelvis, skull, spine, legs).
